analysis.investment_thesis: Central Bank of India is a government-owned PSU bank turnaround that has genuinely recovered — from ₹5,611 Cr in losses (FY19) to ₹3,943 Cr in profits (FY25) — but the hard work is largely done, the revenue growth rate is only 3% CAGR, and 89.27% government ownership structurally limits institutional interest and return potential. At P/E 6.76x and P/B 0.82x it looks cheap, but cheap for a reason.
key_strengths: Profitability restored and accelerating: net profit grew from ₹2,677 Cr (FY24) to ₹3,943 Cr (FY25), a 47% jump reflecting NPA resolution and margin recovery
Other income growing at 12.9% CAGR as fee-based and treasury income diversifies the revenue base
Balance sheet scale: ₹5.05 lakh Cr in assets with deposits growing steadily — provides low-cost funding advantages
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of just 3% over 9 years is that of a slow grower, not a turnaround compounder; core interest income growth depends on credit growth that PSU banks have historically lost to private peers
89.27% government promoter stake means the float is tiny, priority lending mandates constrain returns, and capital allocation decisions are politically influenced
OCF positive in only 1 of the last 5 years — erratic and largely uncontrollable cash generation in a bank scaling up credit
red_flags: Borrowings have grown from ₹5,899 Cr (FY22) to ₹12,929 Cr (FY25) — rapid increase in wholesale funding dependence raises ALM risk
ROE of 11.4% barely clears Lynch's 12% minimum and ROCE is only 5.48%; the business generates adequate but not exciting returns on capital
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Lynch was always skeptical of PSU banks — 'what's the story?' is hard to answer when 89% of the company is owned by the government, lending mandates are set by policy, and the competition from HDFC, ICICI, and Kotak grows fiercer every year. Central Bank has done real work cleaning up its book — going from catastrophic losses to nearly ₹4,000 Cr in profit is genuine progress — but that turnaround story is now largely priced in and the growth engine ahead looks modest.

At P/E 6.76x and P/B 0.82x there's a valuation cushion, which is why I'd hold rather than sell if already invested. But I wouldn't initiate: a 3% revenue CAGR business with government control, thin float, and no differentiated franchise doesn't belong in a GARP portfolio when I can find compounders with PEGs below 1 elsewhere.
